title: Test: Agent Economics
summary: Check what you learned across the whole chapter.

questions.q: The section **The Bill Behind an Accepted Repair** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Owning capacity beats an API at a delivered utilization u* = F / (3600 R (P_eff - v)), not at a token price.
A speedup g applied to a fraction f of the measured critical path gives T' = T[(1-f) + f/g] and a ceiling of 1/(1-f), which a baseline profile reveals before anything is bought.
Measured cost per accepted task is the sum of every initiated task's account, each charge in exactly one category, divided by the distinct tasks accepted under one declared contract.
A one-time adaptation investment recovers its cost after N* = C_adapt / (C_base - C_adapted) tasks, never if the per-task saving is nonpositive, and only while acceptance stays equal.

questions.q: True or false: in the book's concept map, *Cohort cost per accepted task* counts only outcomes accepted under *Task acceptance contract*.
questions.hint: Think about which later idea this concept feeds.
questions.explanation: True. Cohort cost per accepted task counts only outcomes accepted under Task acceptance contract.

questions.q: Which statement captures **Prefix-cache pricing and compaction payback**?
options: Every budget account in the tree keeps budget = settled + reserved + free under atomic, logged transitions, so a delegation tree conserves spending and a stopped child keeps its reservation until its late bills settle.

Accepted tasks per unit time is the platform's deliverable, so sustaining goodput G at acceptance alpha requires admitting G/alpha trajectories and any change that lowers acceptance raises offered load.

Ideal prefix reuse bills the quadratic re-send at the cached rate, which lowers its coefficient without removing it, so a compaction pays back only after enough turns to recover its rewrite and lost cache.
